name: Jade Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, forty-three, and a junior electrician doing house wiring and shop repairs with a supervisor. I took a vocational certificate after years running a school kitchen, and I'm still slower at testing than the others. I like seeing the reason for a fault, though being the oldest person asking the simplest question can feel awkward.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rob drives deliveries, our children are ten and thirteen, and we have a mortgage. My pay is typical for an electrician, we've got five months of expenses saved, and there are a few other electrical firms within reach. I use AI now and then to explain something from my notes, after a colleague has checked the tool; the supervisor still checks the work itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine if the bits that help stay useful. I'd rather learn the trade properly than be told every six weeks that the trade is over. A neat explanation helps me ask a better question; it doesn't make me qualified to skip a check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job and our money feel secure in that picture. My supervisor has been giving me steady paid work, Rob's shifts are regular and five months saved gives us room for a broken appliance. I still have a lot to learn, but that isn't the same as expecting the pay to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised wiring and repair shifts now and through the first year. Once or twice a week I'd check an AI explanation against my course book and ask the supervisor about anything that doesn't match. We'd keep the ordinary mortgage and food budget rather than cut the children's activities for a small change at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with the usual irritation when I need the same test shown twice. I can see a normal week ahead, and I don't need it to be more exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What question would an explanation help you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why the order of a test matters, rather than just what the next step is. If the wording sounds too easy, I take it to the supervisor instead of trying it on a customer's circuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes five months feel enough here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's enough for an ordinary problem while both wages still come in. I wouldn't call it enough to retire or retrain unpaid for years; those are different questions from replacing a fridge.

say: I'd welcome **useful small tools** while learning the trade properly rather than reacting to constant predictions.
I think a **clear explanation** helps me ask questions, not skip a supervisor's check.
think: My **job and money** feel secure with steady supervised shifts and regular household earnings.
Our **five-month reserve** gives us room for an ordinary repair without pretending it funds years without wages.
do: Keep **supervised wiring and repairs** now and through the first year.
Check occasional **AI explanations** against the course book and ask my supervisor about differences.
feel: **Calm**, able to picture an ordinary week while continuing to learn.
S0.quote: I still have a lot to learn, but that isn't the same as expecting the pay to stop.
fieldNote: Her **moderate reserve** supports ordinary security alongside two regular wages, without being portrayed as enough for a long unpaid career change.
Her **occasional tool use** follows a colleague's check and stays subordinate to course material and direct supervision on site.

steps.text: Keep the supervised home wiring and shop repair shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say show us what the new system does to the working day before calling it progress. If it saves time, some of that time should still be used to teach juniors. I'd ask the owner for a straightforward answer about paid learning hours, not take a side because of the software's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if quicker ordering and paperwork let the experienced people cover more jobs without me. A few other firms are nearby, but I'd still need one willing to supervise a learner. Our savings help, though a smaller pay packet would still change what we can spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for a four-week paid trial checking the new AI parts-list tool with my supervisor, after a qualified colleague has tested it. In the first year I'd ask the owner for written learning hours before agreeing to a faster visit rota. At home we'd stop the planned bathroom decoration until we see whether both wages stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I want the numbers rather than another warning. I could live with a different tool more easily than with not knowing how many hours the firm will pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How often the list misses something and how long checking takes, using completed jobs rather than an open live circuit. I'd want the mistakes written down, not quietly fixed and forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the bathroom decision worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About seven hundred we haven't committed yet. The taps work; we can live with the faded paint while we learn whether the pay changes.

say: I'd ask how **the working day** changes before calling a new system progress.
I'd want **paid junior learning** protected even when ordering and paperwork become quicker.
think: My **paid hours could shrink** if experienced electricians can cover more visits without junior help.
Nearby firms only help if one offers **real supervision**, while reduced pay would still affect the household budget.
do: Trial the **AI parts-list tool** for four paid weeks with supervision after qualified colleague testing.
Ask for **written learning hours** before accepting a faster rota during the first year.
Postpone **bathroom decoration** costing about seven hundred while checking both household wages.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, wanting clear paid hours more than another general warning.
S1.quote: I could live with a different tool more easily than with not knowing how many hours the firm will pay me.
fieldNote: The **trial conditions** preserve qualified testing, supervision and paid time, rather than treating a junior as independently responsible for technical decisions.
Delaying **cosmetic spending** is an available household choice because nothing is committed and the existing bathroom still works.

steps.text: Trial the AI parts-list tool for four paid supervised weeks after colleague testing
Postpone seven hundred of uncommitted bathroom decoration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that 2028 changes planning first, with physical robots around 2031. I'd ask what happens to learners while the experienced people take on the new systems. A person can be willing to change and still need someone to pay for the hours of learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose some hours as planning changes, and a lot more if robots take the simpler physical tasks I can do by 2031. I don't know whether that means losing my post altogether. Five months saved helps me avoid a rushed decision, but I still have a mortgage and children to support at forty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd check advertised electrical-service posts and speak to two firms about paid supervised learning, without leaving this job on a verbal promise. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply only where the wage after travel covers our share of the bills and supervision is written down. Rob and I would also review the mortgage terms with the lender now, asking what any temporary payment change would cost before considering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with an urge to get the paperwork in front of me. I haven't decided we're ruined; I have decided that hoping the present rota lasts isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the two firms first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which tasks a junior would be paid to do, who checks them and what hours are guaranteed. A new job isn't safer just because its title has the word service in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Rob's delivery wage stay safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't promise that, especially when robots reach physical work later. We'd use the current wage to work out today's bills, then test the budget with less from each of us rather than declare one person the permanent safety net.

say: I'd explain **planning in 2028** and physical robots around 2031 rather than merge them into one event.
I'd ask who pays for **junior learning hours** while experienced workers use the new systems.
think: I could lose **some hours early** and many more if robots take simpler tasks around 2031.
Our **five-month cushion** buys time, but the mortgage and children still need income when I am forty-eight.
do: Check **advertised service posts** now and ask two firms about paid supervised junior work.
Apply after 2028 only with **written supervision** and wages after travel that cover our household share of bills.
Ask the lender about **mortgage terms** and the full cost of any temporary payment change before considering one.
feel: **Anxious and focused**, comparing real terms without deciding that the household is already ruined.
S2.quote: A new job isn't safer just because its title has the word service in it.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **possible hour losses** from a certain job loss, keeping the mood anxious despite taking the risks seriously.
Her **job comparison** requires actual junior tasks and written supervision, while her partner's physical role is not assumed permanently protected.

steps.text: Apply after 2028 for advertised posts with written supervision and wages covering household share after travel
Ask the lender about temporary mortgage options and their full costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is useful if the training places come with real equipment and paid time. I'd ask our employer to publish those terms instead of sending a list of course links. Families should be able to compare an offer without guessing which bit of the wage disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our income could shrink, but I have longer to become competent before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one, so I can't rely on retirement arriving first. I would rather build one tested skill at a time than chase a new label every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask now for a place on the next small fault-testing class, enrolling only with the firm's fees paid and my normal wage maintained. In the first year after 2031 I'd ask for one supervised service shift a week only if it keeps the same total pay and hours. We'd save another seventy-five a month while both wages and bills allow, reviewing the amount every three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less hurried. I can imagine getting better through a series of paid lessons rather than pretending one certificate solves a ten-year question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the service shift replaces two ordinary shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask how the missing hours are paid before accepting. Learning is useful, but I don't want to hide a pay cut inside the word opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the seventy-five come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keeping the bathroom as it is and buying fewer small things without checking the basket. If school costs or the mortgage payment rise, we'd lower the saving rather than borrow to keep up a target.

say: I'd ask employers for **written paid-training terms** rather than a list of course links.
I'd want families to compare **real wage effects** before agreeing to a course or new duty.
think: Our **income could shrink**, but five years gives me longer to become competent before the planning change.
I'll be **fifty-one in 2034**, so I cannot count on retirement arriving before physical robots.
do: Enrol in **small fault testing** only with employer-paid fees and normal wages maintained.
Seek **one supervised service shift** weekly after 2031 only with the same total pay and hours.
Save **seventy-five monthly** while wages and bills allow, reviewing the target quarterly.
feel: **Anxious but less hurried**, wanting tested skills built through paid lessons.
S3.quote: I don't want to hide a pay cut inside the word opportunity.
fieldNote: Her **service-shift condition** preserves total pay and hours, so a more interesting duty cannot silently replace two ordinary paid shifts.
The **extra saving** can fall when real household costs rise; she does not plan to borrow just to maintain a target.

steps.text: Enrol in fault testing only with employer-paid fees and maintained normal wages
Take supervised service shifts after 2031 only with unchanged total pay and hours
Save seventy-five monthly while wages and bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives the children time to see several kinds of work before choosing. I'd encourage school work visits and proper practical learning, without telling them my trade is the only safe one. I'd still want adult training offers to name the wage, task and instructor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and our money look secure over the next few years in that slower picture. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I'll be fifty-three, and robots follow around 2039 at fifty-six. The children will be older, but I don't know the remaining mortgage or what help they will need, so I wouldn't call the distant end settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same funded fault-testing route now and keep the conditional seventy-five saving plan. This year I'd ask the school for free work visits in different fields for the children, letting them choose what interests them. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual supervised service offers if my hours fall, keeping this job until an affordable written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer future, but not frightened for the next few pay packets. I can let the children talk about their interests without turning dinner into a search for the one safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old would the children be at the thinking-AI date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty and twenty-three in 2036. They might be working or still studying, and I won't put imaginary contributions from them into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in a written offer then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The same things I need now: paid hours, a wage after travel that works and proper supervision for anything I'm still learning. A long warning doesn't mean I can stop reading the conditions.

say: I'd support **varied school work visits** rather than tell the children there is one permanently safe career.
I'd ask adult training offers to name **wage and instruction**, not just an appealing course title.
think: My **near-term job and money** look secure while the major change is still a decade away.
Older children and age fifty-six do not guarantee **a cleared mortgage** or enough income when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Take **funded fault testing** now with fees and normal wages covered, keeping conditional monthly saving.
Ask the school about **free varied work visits** chosen around the children's interests.
Compare **written service offers** after 2036 if hours fall, requiring affordable wages and appropriate supervision.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, while near-term pay feels secure enough for ordinary family conversations.
S4.quote: A long warning doesn't mean I can stop reading the conditions.
fieldNote: She **ages the children** consistently without using their possible future earnings to solve a mortgage budget that remains unknown.
A decade changes **near-term security**, but written pay, travel and supervision conditions still govern any eventual move.

steps.text: Take fault testing only with employer-paid fees and maintained normal wages
Save seventy-five monthly when wages and bills permit
Ask the school about free work visits across fields the children choose
Compare supervised service offers after 2036 if hours fall, checking paid hours and affordable travel-adjusted wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the household could face reduced hours before I have built much practical skill. Paid supervised places with the fee and usual wage covered would help. I'd want employers to put the minimum hours in writing so Rob and I can compare real offers rather than reassuring words.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many different things a family budget is meant to prepare for at once. The boiler, a school cost and a change at work can arrive in the same month. Five months saved is a cushion, not five months in which nothing else can go wrong.

headlineQuote: Five months saved is a cushion, not five months in which nothing else can go wrong.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old junior electrician** with a vocational certificate, learning supervised repair work after school-kitchen employment.
She has **five months saved**, typical pay, some local employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with delivery-driving partner Rob.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleague testing, checking explanations with a course book and supervisor rather than assuming competence.
She feels **secure in AI Plateau**, but possible junior-hour cuts make faster change anxious and training conditional on maintained wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce household hours before she has built enough practical skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid supervised places** should cover fees and usual wages.
**Written minimum hours** would let the household compare actual offers rather than reassurance.
